query:
title: Cant we release an sdk for an old api-version?

question: Hi Azure SDK Onboarding,

My team, AzureStackHCI-VM is working on releasing our sdks for the first time. I recently worked on creating beta sdks for our latest preview api-version (2025-06-01-preview)

Our GA/stable api-version is quite old (2024-01-01) but we want to create an sdk for that as well.
But in this comment, I am told that we are not allowed to release an old sdk version?
https://github.com/Azure/sdk-release-request/issues/6525

What is your recommendation?
ground_truth:
SDK versioning follows a single track and typically allows only forward releases. However, since your earlier versions are all previews, this is not a blocker in your situation.  
The major problem is switching between TypeSpec and Swagger,  which will introduce unexpected breaking changes.
If possible, please consider converting the 2024-01-01 version to TypeSpec and proceed with SDK releases based on that.
If you’re planning to release a new GA version soon, it may be better to skip the stable version and wait for the next GA release. Regarding the s360 flagging, if you’re simply pursuing signoff, I suggest skipping the stable version in Swagger and waiting for your next GA version in TypeSpec.

query:
title: Azure SDK for Microsoft.Applink

question: Hi Team, We are in Private Preview phase for our new RP, Microsoft.Applink and as part of that we have our RP specs in `azure-rest-api-specs-pr` repo - [azure-rest-api-specs-pr/specification/applink/AppLink.Management at RPSaaSMaster · Azure/azure-rest…](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs-pr/tree/RPSaaSMaster/specification/applink/AppLink.Management)
 
We want to be able to work on CLI for our initial set of customers and wondering how to onboard onto azure sdk for the same?

can you please help with the process of generating sdk for RPs in private preview phase? we would want to build up CLI on top of the SDKs.
ground_truth:
**First step:** use the [Azure SDK Tools Agent](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/develop/azsdk-tools-mcp) to create a **Private Preview** release plan with the [manual release-plan flow](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/plan/release-plan-create).
- **For Private Preview:** complete the [API readiness milestone](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/onboard/requirements). **SDK release is not required** at this phase.
- **If you still want SDKs early:** that is allowed, but it is an **internal/private workflow**. Follow the [private-preview SDK FAQ](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/faqs/faqs): generate from the private spec repo, use the private SDK language repos, keep changes on feature branches, and publish only to a private feed if needed.
- **Do not expect a normal public SDK release** until you move to Public Preview/GA. The public self-serve ARM flow is documented in the [management-plane SDK release process](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/plan/mgmt-sdk-release-process).
- **For Azure CLI:** this is a **separate track** from SDK release; the FAQ explicitly says CLI is not part of the SDK release plan.

query:
title: Reusing Release Plans from Preview to GA

question: I have created a release plan for my service for public preview. Can I reuse this release plan for my GA SDK release?
ground_truth:
You cannot simply reuse your public preview release plan for your GA (General Availability) SDK release. Each major milestone (public preview, GA, etc.) requires its own release plan in the Azure SDK Release Planner. The GA release plan will have additional requirements, such as more comprehensive testing, additional samples, and potentially a final architecture review. You should create a new release plan specifically for your GA SDK release to ensure all required steps and validations are tracked and completed. The release planner helps you track your progress and ensures you meet all the prerequisites for a GA release.
However, you can use your public preview release plan as a reference or template to speed up the creation of your GA release plan, but it is important to go through the official process and create a dedicated GA plan.
If you have already completed some steps during public preview (such as generating SDKs or completing reviews), those may not need to be repeated, but you must still document and track them in the GA release plan.

query:
title: SDK Breaking change trigger

question: Hi,
If we merge our swaggers to public main and then find the need to make changes, for example in our client tsp, or corrections in our swagger, what is the process? We are needing to merge main for API docs to become available, but take an extension on SDK generation for our public preview release, and I want to ensure that if we do happen to find some changes to make SDK side what we can expect to trigger various processes and cause delays for us.
Thank you in advance!
ground_truth:
Submit subsequent specification or client.tsp changes through a new public spec PR, complete applicable validation/reviews, and regenerate and revalidate affected SDKs. SDK-only client customization differs from an on-the-wire correction to a published API version: the latter is subject to API-versioning/breaking-change policy and may require a new API version rather than an in-place edit.
For TypeSpec management-plane SDKs, merging the public spec PR automatically generates SDKs for supported languages and links SDK PRs to the release plan. Confirm the service plane and source format rather than generalizing this automation to every Swagger/data-plane workflow. Current SDK development guidance requires Swagger/OpenAPI services to convert to TypeSpec before SDK generation/release.
Generation is not publication. Review/test generated SDK changes and meet release prerequisites before merging SDK PRs; their merge triggers package release in the automatic TypeSpec management-plane flow. Coordinate the SDK extension with release owners: do not assume public spec merges leave generation entirely manual. Corrections can require regeneration and renewed review, causing delays.

query:
title: Fixing Invalid Type Specifications and SDK Regeneration in Released APIs

question: Hi Azure SDK Onboarding,
Our team found an invalid type specification in our previous 2 API releases (1 preview, 1 stable).  I've read through (lightly) the breaking change deep dive, which looks like I'll have to reach out to the review board to get their approval, however, I was wondering what is the recommended way to implement a fix for existing APIs, up to the point where it can be reviewed by ARM and Breaking changes board.
Normally, I would create a branch, commit a base version for review, then create a release plan against the new branch (then add in changes, get ARM sign off, then request the sdk release).
How do I regenerate the SDKs once I have a fix in place for the previously released verisons?  Will they require manual updates (e.g. create a PR in each sdk repo with a fix)?
Any guidance would be appreciated!
ground_truth:
Assuming this is an ARM / management-plane API authored in TypeSpec, the usual path is:
- Fix the released API version in the spec first and treat it as a bug-fix correction if the change makes the spec match the service's already-shipped behavior. If your PR gets BreakingChangeReviewRequired or VersioningReviewRequired, follow the breaking change review process (aka.ms/brch); Versioning-Approved-BugFix may apply for this scenario.
- Complete ARM review after the breaking change review is resolved. You cannot proceed to ARM review until the breaking change process is complete.
- After the spec fix is approved and merged, create a new release plan in the release planner and submit a generate SDK request. The automation creates a GitHub issue assigned to Copilot, which generates draft PRs in each language repo (Java, JavaScript, Python, Go). No manual fix PR per SDK repo is needed for pure generated changes.
- Service owners verify the draft PRs, click Ready for review when satisfied, and are responsible for addressing feedback and merging.
- For .NET, service owners must generate the SDK manually and submit a PR to azure-sdk-for-net themselves.
- Manual repo work is only needed if a language-specific handwritten layer also needs adjustment.

query:
title: TypeSpec SDK API Reviews Process for Management Plane Services

question: Hello General,
First time working on typespec. I'm from Compute team and this is my api-specs PR to add a new preview API version: Add 2025-07-01-preview API version to Azure Fleet by diyellap · Pull Request #36207 · Azure/azure-rest-api-specs.
It has autogenerated SDK API reviews. How to get these reviewed by specific SDK teams?
ground_truth:
Welcome to the TypeSpec and Azure SDK onboarding process! Since you are working on a new preview API version and have generated the SDKs (autogenerated SDK API reviews), here is how you get these reviewed by the specific SDK teams:
Management Plane (ARM) SDKs Do NOT Require Arch Board Review:
For management plane (ARM) libraries like Azure Fleet, you do NOT need to schedule an SDK Architecture Board meeting. The review process is handled through the pull request (PR) workflow in the Azure REST API Specs repository.
SDK Review Process for Your Scenario:
After your REST API spec PR is approved and merged, the next steps are:
Ensure you have a release plan created in the Azure SDK Release Planner.
The SDK generation and release planning will involve tracking the release plan milestones, where you can monitor which language SDKs are being generated and when they are ready for review.
Assigning Specific SDK Teams as Reviewers:
SDK teams are automatically assigned as reviewers for their respective language repos using the CODEOWNERS file in each SDK repository. If your service is not already listed in the CODEOWNERS file for a given language SDK repo, you should add your service and the appropriate GitHub users or teams to ensure SDK team visibility and review (see the reference for details).
You can also @-mention specific SDK team members in the generated SDK PRs in each language repository if you need urgent attention.
How to Track and Request Review:
After the SDK PR is generated (either manually or via automation), monitor the PR in the respective SDK repo. The SDK team responsible for that language will review according to the CODEOWNERS assignment.
If you do not see timely review or need to escalate, reach out to the language-specific Teams channel or the SDK repo maintainers directly.
Summary of Steps:
Confirm your service is listed in the CODEOWNERS file for each SDK repo.
Create/track your release plan in the Azure SDK Release Planner.
Monitor and follow up on the generated SDK PRs for reviews.
For Management Plane, no Arch Board meeting is needed; reviews are handled via the PR process.
Let me know if you need guidance on updating CODEOWNERS or navigating the release planner!
References below provide detailed steps and process links.

query:
title: Target Branch Selection for Onboarding New Resource Types

question: General I have created a PR to onboard new resource types. Is main the right target branch?
I was suggested to use azure-rest-api-specs-pr/RPSaaSMaster (private) Or azure-rest-api-specs/main (public) as the target branch?
I am getting branch protection error with the current PR.
Thank you for the help!
ground_truth:
When onboarding new resource types (especially for ARM/Control Plane APIs), the right target branch depends on the stage of your API and whether your work should be public or private:
If your resource types are still under development or in private preview (not ready for public visibility), you should target the RPSaaSMaster branch in the private repo: azure-rest-api-specs-pr.
Once your API is ready for public preview or GA, you should target the main branch in the public repo: azure-rest-api-specs.
You mentioned getting a branch protection error. This is likely because the main branch in the private repo is read-only and mirrored from the public repo. You cannot merge directly into main in the private repo. For private work, use RPSaaSMaster. For public release, use main in the public repo.
Summary:
Use azure-rest-api-specs-pr/RPSaaSMaster for private onboarding and early-stage work.
Use azure-rest-api-specs/main for public onboarding and final publishing.
If you need to update your PR, change the target branch to RPSaaSMaster in the private repo for onboarding new resource types. If your resource is ready for public consumption, move it to a PR against the public repo's main branch.
Let me know if you need help updating your PR or have questions about the process!
